summary:
Western Sahara is a disputed territory with no single legal order running through it. Morocco controls most of the ground and Moroccan security services, courts and detention facilities operate there; the Sahrawi Arab Democratic Republic claims sovereignty and governs through exile institutions and refugee camps in Algeria. Which framework a visitor stands under depends on which part of the territory they are in.

Moroccan jurisdiction reaches into the territory in practice. On 9 December 2005 Human Rights Watch reported the trial of seven human-rights defenders from Moroccan-controlled Western Sahara on charges of fomenting illegal protests, called the charges dubious and demanded a fair trial. The case shows Moroccan courts and detention operating on Sahrawi political cases, not only on paper.

Same-sex intimacy is criminalised under both frameworks. Moroccan law carries six months to three years of imprisonment. For the Sahrawi Arab Democratic Republic, the Council for Global Equality, Equaldex and ILGA record same-sex sexual activity as illegal for both men and women, punishable by up to three years, and a July 2017 PinkNews roundup listed the SADR among jurisdictions where homosexuality is illegal for men and women and had been for decades. A trans visitor in a relationship that local law would read as same-sex under birth-sex status therefore stands inside a criminal prohibition in either part of the territory.

The SADR's own position is contested. In 2010 Ahmed Mulay Alli, the SADR's diplomatic representative in Mexico, said the Constitution 'does not refer to homosexuality or any other sexual practice... it does not punish it'. The Spanish Commission for Refugee Aid (CEAR) reads the same silence as leaving LGBTQ people with no legal protection against discrimination or violence. Constitutional silence is not decriminalisation, and no statute in the inventory decriminalises anything.

The only documented account of the Sahrawi authorities applying such charges comes from a 2009 USCRI report: officials running the refugee camps in Algeria said they were holding some prisoners on 'homosexuality' charges while alleging facts that would more fittingly describe rape. The charge sits in the hands of camp administration rather than a court.

Social exposure is high. Most residents are Muslim, and relationships between people of the same sex are widely read as a foreign phenomenon.

No source in the inventory records a trans-specific statute, a protection mechanism, or a documented case of a trans visitor being processed under either framework.
tangentialFactors:
The territory was under Spanish colonial rule until 1976, and homosexuality was not decriminalised in Spain until 1979. That inheritance predates the Moroccan and Sahrawi frameworks that now compete over the ground.

The two frameworks diverge in form. Moroccan law states a penalty of six months to three years. International monitors record the Sahrawi Arab Democratic Republic as criminalising same-sex activity for both men and women with a penalty of up to three years, while the SADR's own diplomatic representative has described its Constitution as silent on the question. The SADR claims sovereignty but governs through exile institutions and refugee camps in Algeria rather than through courts on the ground in Western Sahara, so its criminalisation is documented in the camps and in the monitors' listings rather than in proceedings a visitor would encounter inside the territory.
localsOnly:
Residents of the territory live under the same criminalisation a visitor does. Moroccan courts and detention operate on Sahrawi political cases: the seven human-rights defenders tried from 9 December 2005 faced charges of fomenting illegal protests that Human Rights Watch called dubious.

For Sahrawi refugees in the camps in Algeria, the 2009 USCRI report records camp officials holding prisoners on 'homosexuality' charges while alleging facts that would more fittingly describe rape, a charge administered by camp authorities rather than decided by a court.

The Spanish Commission for Refugee Aid states there is no type of protection for LGBTQ individuals in case of discrimination or violence. Most residents are Muslim, and relationships between people of the same sex are widely read as a foreign phenomenon.
outOfScopeNotes:
No source in the inventory records a trans-specific statute, a protection mechanism, or a documented case of a trans visitor or trans resident being processed under either framework. Whether either authority would apply a same-sex provision to a trans person, and on what reading of that person's legal sex, is not sourced.

Document and marker rules, facilities access, and trans-specific medical care are not addressed by any source in the inventory for this territory.

The SADR's constitutional silence is not decriminalisation. No statute in the inventory decriminalises same-sex activity under either framework, and the 2010 diplomatic statement is a position rather than a legal text.
